Right, three things on the economy and then I will let you eat. First, the number everybody quoted last week was a valuation, not a price, and a valuation is somebody's opinion with a decimal point in it. Second, when people say the market is liquid they mean you can sell without moving the price, and that is a very different question from whether the thing is worth anything. And third, on the bubble question, which somebody always asks me. I would rather not use the word bubble at all. Every bubble is obvious afterwards and invisible while you are inside it, and anybody who tells you they can see one from the inside is selling something. What I would say is this. If you cannot explain where the yield is coming from, you had better assume you are the yield.

Here is something nobody explains to people who move between countries, and it costs them at every dinner. In English, and particularly in American English, you can talk about money for an hour without ever mentioning your own. The subject is the economy, the market, the currency, the policy. It is never how much you have, what you paid for the house, or what you earned before you stopped. Asking any of those things is not rude in the way that shouting is rude. It is rude in a quieter way. It puts the other person in a position where every possible answer is uncomfortable. The rule is simple once you see it. Talk about money in the third person. Numbers about the world are conversation. Numbers about the people at the table are an intrusion, and the only person who may safely bring up your finances is you.
